WebsterInternational GerrymanderingAlthough gerrymandering is a particularly American phenomenon, the territorial manipulation of districts has been used to gain or maintain power in many countries such as the United Kingdom, Chile, Hungary, Australia, and Kuwait, among many others. In Canada, for example, the most infamous case pertained to the constituencies of Alberta and Saskatchewan after their creation as provinces in 1905. The boundaries of the original districts had been drawn to favor the Liberal Party and to elect provincial governments from that party. Since 1964, the responsibility to draw districts has been held by nonpartisan Elections Canada, and there has been little controversy over gerrymandering.Gerrymandering is more common and accepted in France where there is little or no governmental or judicial oversight. For example, in the 1993 elections, 80% of seats were won with only 58% of the votes. In the United Kingdom, “gerrymandering” was employed to influence the results for Northern Ireland after Home Rule was granted in 1921, but in the wider United Kingdom and in many other countries, the principal means of electoral manipulation is from malapportionment, or the unequal population of districts which can be quite extreme. In 2017, the largest House of Commons constituency in the United Kingdom was more than five times the size of the smallest.View chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780081022955102665Reference work2020, International Encyclopedia of Human Geography (Second Edition)Richard Morrill, Gerald R. MorrillIntroductionGerrymandering refers to the deliberate manipulation of territory to gain disproportionate power in elections. The term ‘gerrymandering’ immortalizes the name of the Massachusetts governor, and the name of the cartoonist, Tisdale, who in 1821 likened the shape of one manipulated district to a salamander (Figure 1). The purpose of gerrymandering is to help ‘your side’ and to hurt the ‘other side’, whether this refers to political party, a racial or ethnic group, kinds of territory (urban, rural, suburban, rich, poor), or individuals (incumbents or challengers), and thereby to obtain a higher share of seats than of votes.Sign in to download full-size imageFigure 1. The original Gerrymander (1812).While the most publicized examples of gerrymandering recently have bizarrely shaped congressional districts (see examples below), gerrymandering is practiced at all levels of government in which there are electoral districts with single members – legislatures, county and city councils, and many others. And clever map drawers can gerrymander – that is successfully discriminate – without resorting to extreme irregularity.Show moreView chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780080449104007793Reference work2009, International Encyclopedia of Human GeographyR. WebsterAbstract“Gerrymandering” refers to the deliberate manipulation of territory toward predetermining the winner in elections and has particular relevance to the United States though the practice occurs in other countries as well. Gerrymandering commonly involves the marginalization of groups of voters such as ethnic minorities or working-class communities. Less frequently, there are also instances of affirmative gerrymandering that seek to redress the effects of underrepresentation. Gerrymandering has a long history dating back to the 19th century and remains a significant concern within electoral processes in the United States, evidenced in a number of judicial reviews in recent elections.View chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780081022955102665Reference work2020, International Encyclopedia of Human Geography (Second Edition)Richard Morrill, Gerald R. MorrillExamples of GerrymanderingMany wonderful and egregious examples of gerrymandering are widely viewable on websites (please see the section entitled ‘Relevant website’). Monmonier's book, Bushmanders and Bullwinkles, shows several. Also look at the US Congressional District Atlas. Two famous examples of rather irregular gerrymandering are reproduced here. Figure 3 shows part of the recent and court-approved Texas redistricting plan and Figure 4 the famous original 1992 North Carolina congressional district plan, and its notorious first and twelfth districts – racial gerrymanders.Sign in to download full-size imageFigure 3. Racial gerrymandering in Mississippi.Sign in to download full-size imageFigure 4. The famous North Carolina 12th District.While gerrymandering often does take the form of extremely irregular districts, subtler gerrymandering can appear reasonably compact, while using any one of these four tools. Changes to the congressional districts of Mississippi illustrate the transition from traditional communities to a historic discriminatory gerrymander against black voters, by splitting the north to south trending community via east–west districts (Figure 5). Similarly, Republican districters have sometimes been able to reduce democratic representation to a single ‘packed’ core seat, while splitting the remaining democratic vote area into several surrounding districts, each with a majority of suburban Republicans (e.g., Minneapolis, Atlanta, Dallas, Houston).Sign in to download full-size imageFigure 5. WebsterHow to GerrymanderThere are various means of gerrymandering electoral districts (see Fig. 2):Sign in to download full-size imageFigure 2. How to gerrymander.1.Splitting or the dilution of concentrations of the other side, so as to leave them a minority in as many districts as possible; cracking is a form in which the district of an incumbent of the other party is split.2.Packing or concentrating the other side in as few districts as possible, so that many of their votes are “wasted,” while also creating many districts with moderate margins for your side.3.Placing incumbents of the other side in the same revised districts.4.Creating multimember districts where your party is in the majority.Dilution is effective where the other party has enough support in one area to elect one representative, but splitting can prevent any representation. Packing is the ideal tool where the other party has enough votes—in a region or metropolis—to elect two or more representatives. Carving a district out of the densest central concentration will pack minority party voters so that they receive 85%–90% of the vote, thereby “wasting” 35%–40%.Placing two incumbents of the other party in revised districts was a key component of the infamous DeLay, Texas redistricting. Multimember districts in which one party has a majority were historically an effective way of preventing minority representation. This strategy includes, for example, minimizing Black representation in local and state government, mainly in the south, but it also works for partisan discrimination, as in the Indiana legislature (Indianapolis).Most gerrymanders are executed by the very legislative bodies they control, the state legislature, city council, or county commission, an obvious but accepted conflict of interest, but even bipartisan commissions or state or federal courts are not immune from the temptation and practice. At the very least, courts routinely approve gerrymanders, no matter how extreme.Show moreView chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780081022955102665Reference work2020, International Encyclopedia of Human Geography (Second Edition)Richard Morrill, Gerald R. WebsterGerrymandering and the CourtsGerrymandering was rarely challenged before the late 1960s, in part because it was simply accepted as “politics as usual” and also because it was not as outrageous or as necessary. Malapportionment, or unequal population among districts, was by far the more obviously unfair form of electoral discrimination, and even this action was not struck down by the US Supreme Court until 1962 (Baker v. Carr).The US courts have both condemned and endorsed gerrymandering, but only with respect to discrimination against a racial or linguistic minority. How can this be? Gerrymandering was considered “just politics” until critical decisions on the basis of the Voting Rights Act (1965 and subsequent amendments), which outlawed racial vote dilution, disallowed retrogression, and required “preclearance” of plans by the Department of Justice in states with a history of racial discrimination. The most definitive decision was Thornburg v. Gingles (1986), which established the standard that race can be one but not the only factor in drawing a district, but that it is reasonable to design “majority–minority” districts where practicable. The basic problem with race-conscious districting was the risk of packing in the large urban ghettoes and of extreme irregularity in assembling sufficient minority numbers in rural and small-city parts of the south. The one criterion of racial representation was elevated at the expense of others, such as compactness or nonracial communities of interest.The Department of Justice, many state legislatures, and the courts began the 1990s round of redistricting with the expectation of striving for proportionality, even if extreme affirmative gerrymandering was required. This led to the creation of well-publicized irregularities in many redistricting plans, with disparate parts connected by strips of interstate highway, as in the North Carolina's 12th congressional district (Fig. 4). The gerrymandered districts did elect a record number of minority group members in the 1992 elections, but at the expense of any geographic semblance of community. Voters in several states filed actions against plans. In the majority of such cases, the Supreme Court did reject the plans as unconstitutional racial gerrymanders, and required less draconian plans (Turner v. State of Arkansas). Yet several other infamously irregular plans were found to be acceptable.Developments Since 2010The 2010 US census, providing populations in time for redistricting and the 2012 elections, led to a massive manipulation of boundaries for congress, state legislatures, and other units of government using districts. The 2010 elections were highly favorable for the Republican Party, being off-year and having brought out populist nonmetropolitan reaction to Democratic “excess”, and the Republicans gained 64 seats. The 2011–12 district drawing led to a substantial level of gerrymandering, helping Republicans gain seats in several states and to protect seats already won. In the 2012 elections, gerrymandering helped Republicans most in the states listed in Table 1 (percent of seats won versus percent of votes noted). But Democrats probably were helped by gerrymandering in Maryland, Illinois, and perhaps California.Table 1. Republican gains from gerrymandering, 2012 electionStateProbgerrym% Seats% VotesNorth Carolina26949Pennsylvania1–27249Michigan16447Florida16253Ohio27552Indiana17754Virginia17341The imbalance between seats won versus votes received is high in several other states, and higher than the probable gerrymanders in the states as illustrated in Table 1. The reason is simply the “bad” geography of partisan voters. Democratic voters are concentrated in larger metropolitan areas, where districts drawn fairly still leads to millions of “wasted” votes but fewer than would be expected if seats were proportional in Missouri, Kentucky, South Carolina, Alabama, Arkansas, and even Idaho, Nebraska, Kansas, and Oklahoma. Conversely, Republican voters are too dispersed in several states to form a winnable district, likely in California, Maryland, Massachusetts, and perhaps in New York, Connecticut, Maine, Minnesota, Oregon, and Washington.The gerrymandering in 2011–12 caused imbalance between votes won and seats won and led to strong movements for reform and to several lawsuits, several of which are still going on. Fairer representation to overcome imbalance due to excessive concentration and dispersion would ironically require the purposeful gerrymandering of single-member districts. The solution for these is the use of multimember districts with employment of rank-choice voting, as is now used in a few cities such as Minneapolis.Recent and Ongoing Court CasesAs of April 2018, only 2 years before the census and redistricting process begins again in 2020–21, there are at least eight states with ongoing litigation, at times including multiple suits in the same state. Arguably, the amount of litigation has increased due to the Supreme Court's 2013 decision in Shelby County v. Holder which resulted in the negation of the preclearance process. This means that discriminatory districting plans are no longer rejected by the Department of Justice before implementation, but rather must be challenged in court. Notably, the majority of the currently ongoing cases pertain to partisan gerrymandering (Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia, Michigan) with racial gerrymandering ongoing in four states (North Carolina, Texas, Virginia, Arizona). The case law pertaining to partisan gerrymandering is quite limited with the courts wishing to avoid the “political thicket” in the past. As a result, the decisions in those ongoing cases pertaining to partisan gerrymandering could have dramatic effects on future redistricting cycles.Wisconsin: Gill v. WhitfordArguably, the case with the greatest potential to have a major effect on the next round of redistricting is Gill v. Whitford in Wisconsin. The case pertains to Wisconsin's 2011 state assembly districts which were declared an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander in November 2016 by a three-judge federal panel. The panel found that the Republican plan violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause and the First Amendment's freedom of association (Brennan Center 2018).The three federal judge panel found that the 2011 Republican map had both a discriminatory intent and discriminatory effect upon Democrats in Wisconsin. Supporting evidence included the fact that Democrats won a majority of the votes in state assembly races in both 2012 and 2014, but Republicans won 60 or more of the 99 seats in the chamber. The state of Wisconsin appealed the decision to the US Supreme Court which heard oral arguments on October 3, 2017. A stay was also granted to keep the current districts in place while the Court reviews the case. A final decision is expected in June 2018, but the Supreme Court declined to make a decision.Pennsylvania: League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania v. Commonwealth of PennsylvaniaThree lawsuits (two in federal court and one in state court) are challenging Pennsylvania's 2011 congressional map as an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander, alleging that Republicans used their legislative control to crack and pack Democratic-affiliated voters into specific districts in order to minimize the representation of Democratic voters.In June 2017, the League of Women Voters filed suit in state court against the Republican drawn 2011 Pennsylvania congressional districts based on the state constitution, claiming the map was an illegal partisan gerrymander. A central element of plaintiff's argument was that those drawing the map in 2011 used political data to improve the odds that the GOP would remain dominant in the state legislature. In January 2018, the Pennsylvania State Supreme Court invalidated the map as a partisan gerrymander under the state's constitution, enjoined the state from using the map in the November 2018 legislative elections, and ordered the state to redraw its congressional districts. Because the state failed to draw new district boundaries, the court adopted a new plan for use in the upcoming congressional elections.Two additional suits have been filed in federal court. The first, Corman v. Torres, was filed in federal court by Republican members of Congress and the state legislature to stop the state Supreme Court's new districts from being used in the November 2018 elections. In March 2018, the lawsuit was dismissed by a three-judge federal panel on multiple bases, including that Republican members of Congress from Pennsylvania had not suffered any injury from the state Supreme Court's decision.The second suit was filed by four Pennsylvania voters in federal court arguing the state's 2011 congressional districts were an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander and violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments to the US Constitution. The court declined to hear the case, remains active with ongoing discussion over jurisdiction, but should conclude in May 2018. Plaintiffs have filed an appeal with the US Supreme Court, and it remains to be seen if the Court will hear the case.Unresolved IssuesThere are two aspects of gerrymandering and electoral fairness in the United States left unresolved: those of party and of territory (e.g., urban, suburban, and rural-small town). At present there is no consensus in the American court system for how to identify and invalidate manipulation in the redistricting process against a political party or recognized place or community, though some guidance for identifying partisan gerrymandering may result from ongoing litigation. Compactness and communities of interest are viewed as “desirable” but not as essential. Courts have ruled against recognition of any kind of community except race or language and have accepted blatant and intentional political gerrymanders. Although the courts reference inexcusable irregularity in striking down a racial gerrymander, they totally fail to be concerned with convoluted districts that are political (Badham v. Eu, Bandemer v. Davis).In the 1990s, 2000s, and 2010s rounds of redistricting, Republicans, when in control, ingeniously pursued creating racial majority–minority districts, frequently eliminating liberal white Democrats. The most extreme case after 2000 was in Texas, where the Republicans replaced a court-drawn plan, leading to a massive shift of seats to the Republicans. The plan was upheld at all levels, revealing that the United States has not been ready to tackle the unfairness of partisan gerrymandering, no matter how seriously it disenfranchises voters, in a winner-take-all electoral system. Given the ongoing litigation over the issue of partisan gerrymandering, judicial relief may come prior to the next round of redistricting in 2021.What is fairness and why does it matter? Fair representation means that citizens' votes are meaningful, that over time and over a small set of districts, the shares of seats won is proportional to the share of votes received, and that some peoples' votes are not weightier than others. The problems with gerrymandered districts which violate this sense of fair representation include distrust of government, apathy, not voting and withdrawal from the political process, lack of competition, and lack of change in representation even when voter preferences shift. Lack of competition results in many districts with no opponents even willing to run. The further risk is nonresponsiveness and corruption of government.Gerrymandering, Computers, and Geographic Information SystemParty workers have always used a combination of maps and knowledge of returns by voter precincts to accomplish their gerrymandering. The geographic information system (GIS) revolution in geography has also created a revolution in redistricting and therefore in gerrymandering technology in two respects. First was the development of computer cartography, in turn dependent on the creation of digital line (boundary) files, and second was the extension of the census down to the block level nationwide. The availability of data at the block level, together with efficient and interactive GIS packages, ironically made it far easier to carry out ever more egregious gerrymanders, for example, by using stretches of highway to connect disparate parts of a district. At the same time, excellent programming models exist which could draw fair and compact districts. The best models achieve not only political fairness between political parties but also compactness and respect for communities of interest and the integrity of political boundaries; these are almost never used in contemporary electoral districting in the United States.Show moreView chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780081022955102665Reference work2020, International Encyclopedia of Human Geography (Second Edition)Richard Morrill, Gerald R.
